raw_text:
**Introduction and Epidemiology**
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a rare, life-threatening form of idiopathic systolic heart failure that manifests during late pregnancy or the early postpartum months [1–3]. Defined by a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) under 45% in the absence of pre-existing cardiac disease [4,5], PPCM represents a major driver of maternal cardiovascular mortality globally [1,6]. While the global incidence is approximately 1 in 2000 live births, significant ethnic and geographical disparities persist [1,6]. The incidence is exceptionally high in Haiti (1 in 300) [5,6] and Nigeria (1 in 100) [6]. In the United States, Black ancestry is associated with a fourfold higher risk of developing PPCM and a lower likelihood of myocardial recovery compared to other populations [7,8]. Major predisposing risk factors include hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, multiparity, advanced maternal age, and multiple gestations [3,9].

**Pathophysiology**
Bench-to-bedside research has established a "two-hit" model integrating vasculo-hormonal triggers and genetic susceptibility [3,6]. During late pregnancy, systemic oxidative stress upregulates cardiac cathepsin D, which cleaves the hormone prolactin into a cardiotoxic, angiostatic, and proapoptotic 16 kDa subfragment [10]. This 16 kDa fragment triggers the expression of microRNA-146a, driving microvascular damage and cardiomyocyte apoptosis [11]. Concurrently, late-gestation placental secretion of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1), a vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibitor, creates a systemic anti-angiogenic state that impairs cardiac homeostasis [12], particularly when accentuated by preeclampsia [12,13]. Furthermore, up to 20% of PPCM patients harbor pathogenic gene variants typical of familial dilated cardiomyopathy [14,15]. Truncating mutations in the titin gene (*TTN*) are the most commonly implicated, alongside mutations in sarcomeric and cytoskeletal genes like *BAG3*, *MYH7*, and *MYBPC3* [14–16].

**Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis**
Early clinical recognition is crucial but frequently delayed because typical heart failure symptoms (e.g., dyspnea, fatigue, and peripheral edema) mimic the physiological discomforts of normal late pregnancy [3,4]. Delayed diagnosis is strongly correlated with worse baseline LVEF and lower recovery rates [4,17]. Transthoracic echocardiography is the diagnostic standard, confirming left ventricular systolic dysfunction [18,19]. Serum brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) or N-terminal pro-BNP (NT-proBNP) levels serve as highly sensitive biomarkers to differentiate acute heart failure from normal gestational changes [18,20].

**Management**
Therapeutic strategies require a coordinated cardio-obstetrics team [3]. Pharmacological management of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) must prioritize maternal-fetal safety [21]. During pregnancy, standard medications such as angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs), and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) are strictly contraindicated due to severe fetotoxicity [18,22,23]. Afterload reduction during gestation is safely achieved with hydralazine and nitrates, while beta-1 selective blockers and loop diuretics are used cautiously under fetal surveillance [23,24]. Postpartum, full guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) can be optimized, although safety data during lactation are currently lacking for newer agents such as ARNIs and SGLT2 inhibitors [23,24].

Targeting the prolactin pathway, the dopamine agonist bromocriptine has emerged as a disease-modifying therapy [10,25,26]. A landmark multicenter randomized trial demonstrated that adding bromocriptine to standard HFrEF therapy significantly improves LVEF recovery [26], a finding recently supported by registry data from the ESC EORP PPCM cohort [27]. Concomitant therapeutic anticoagulation is mandatory during bromocriptine use to mitigate peripartum hypercoagulability and prothrombotic risks [22,28]. For patients with severe cardiogenic shock, short-term mechanical circulatory support (MCS) using intra-aortic balloon pumps or veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) is utilized to maintain systemic perfusion [29,30]. Wearable cardioverter-defibrillators (WCD) are highly beneficial in bridging the temporary risk of sudden cardiac death during the early arrhythmogenic phase of the disease [17].

**Prognosis and Subsequent Pregnancies**
PPCM has a higher rate of myocardial recovery than other non-ischemic cardiomyopathies, with 50% to 70% of patients recovering an LVEF ≥50% within six months postpartum [19,21]. However, a subset of patients progresses to end-stage heart failure requiring durable left ventricular assist devices (LVAD) or heart transplantation [29,30]. Extensive counseling regarding future pregnancies is paramount [7,21]. For women with persistent left ventricular dysfunction (LVEF <50%), subsequent pregnancy is contraindicated due to extremely high risks of clinical relapse and maternal death [7,21]. Even among women who achieve complete LVEF recovery, there remains a 20% to 30% risk of heart failure recurrence in subsequent gestations, necessitating detailed pre-conception planning and multidisciplinary monitoring [7,21].
